candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A shareholder of a company pays Rs 5,000 towards a call that the directors have not yet made. How should the company treat this amount?

options.text: Credit it to Share Capital A/c immediately and treat it as part of owners' equity
Credit it to Calls in Arrears A/c and show it as an asset of the company
Credit it to Calls in Advance A/c and treat it as a liability until the call falls due
Credit it to Securities Premium Reserve A/c as a capital reserve of the company

candidate.explanation: The excerpt states that money received before a call is made is 'Calls in Advance', which is a liability of the company and is credited to Calls in Advance Account, then adjusted when the call becomes due. Option A is wrong because the amount is a liability, not yet share capital. Option B is wrong because Calls in Arrears is a debit balance representing unpaid calls, not money received. Option D is wrong because no premium is involved; the amount is received against a future call.

learning_objective.objective: Explain the accounting treatment of calls received in advance.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A shareholder failed to pay a call of Rs 4,000 on the due date and paid it after 6 months. The Articles of Association are silent on interest, so Table F applies, and the company charges interest at the maximum rate Table F permits on calls in arrears. How much interest is payable by the shareholder?

options.text: Rs 240
Rs 200
Rs 400
Rs 480

candidate.explanation: Per the excerpt, when the Articles are silent Table F permits interest not exceeding 10% p.a. on unpaid amounts for the period between the due date and actual payment. Interest = 4,000 x 10% x 6/12 = Rs 200. Rs 240 uses 12%, which is the Table F ceiling for calls in advance, not arrears. Rs 400 and Rs 480 ignore the 6-month period and charge a full year at 10% and 12% respectively.

learning_objective.objective: Compute interest on calls in arrears under Table F.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A company issued 100 shares of Rs 10 each at a premium of Rs 2 per share. The premium was fully received along with the allotment money. A shareholder holding these shares then failed to pay the first call, and the directors forfeited the shares. What is the correct treatment of Securities Premium Reserve at the time of forfeiture?

options.text: It is debited with Rs 200 together with Share Capital A/c, as the premium is lost
It is debited with Rs 100, being half the premium, and Share Capital A/c with the rest
It is debited with Rs 200 and Bank A/c is credited to refund the premium
It is not debited, because the premium was received and the forfeiture amount excludes the premium

candidate.explanation: The excerpt states that when shares issued at a premium are forfeited and the premium has been received, Securities Premium Reserve is not debited and the amount of forfeiture excludes the premium. Here the premium was fully received on allotment, so options A and B, which debit it, and option C, which debits it with a refund, are all contradicted. The excerpt requires a debit to Securities Premium Reserve only for premium not received.

learning_objective.objective: Apply the rule for forfeiture of shares issued at a premium.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: The profits of a firm for the last three years were Rs 30,000, Rs 36,000 and Rs 42,000. Goodwill is to be valued at 4 years' purchase of the average profits of these three years. What is the value of goodwill?
candidate.explanation: The excerpt values goodwill by multiplying past average profits by the agreed number of years. Average profit = (30,000 + 36,000 + 42,000) / 3 = Rs 36,000, and goodwill = 36,000 x 4 = Rs 1,44,000. Rs 36,000 omits the multiplier, Rs 1,08,000 is just the total of the three years' profits, and Rs 4,32,000 multiplies that total by 4 instead of the average.

learning_objective.objective: Value goodwill of a partnership firm by the average profits method.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: A partnership firm maintains partners' capitals under the fixed capital method. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: Capital accounts change every year as profit share, interest and drawings are recorded in them
Capital accounts show a credit balance that stays fixed unless capital is added or withdrawn by agreement
Current accounts always show a credit balance and appear only on the liabilities side
A debit balance in a partner's current account is shown on the liabilities side of the balance sheet

candidate.explanation: The excerpt states that under the fixed capital method capital accounts always show a credit balance that remains the same unless capital is introduced or withdrawn. Option A is wrong because profit share, interest and drawings go to the Current Account. Options C and D are wrong because a current account may show a debit or credit balance, and a debit balance is shown on the assets side.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish fixed capital and current accounts of partners.

candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: X and Y share profits in the ratio 3:2. They admit Z, and the new profit sharing ratio of X, Y and Z becomes 5:3:2. The agreement does not say in what ratio Z acquires his share from X and Y. What is the sacrificing ratio of X and Y?
candidate.explanation: The new partner is assumed to acquire his share from the old partners in their old profit sharing ratio, so the sacrificing ratio of X and Y is the same as their old ratio of 3:2. The new ratio 5:3 of X and Y is only the ratio of their retained shares and 2:3 is the reverse of the old ratio, so neither can be the sacrifice.

learning_objective.syllabus_unit: Partnership Accounts: Admission of a Partner
learning_objective.objective: Compute the sacrificing ratio when the new ratio is given.

Securities Premium Reserve A/c; shown under Reserves and Surpluses
Statement of Profit and Loss; shown as other income
Share Capital A/c; shown under Share Capital in equity

The premium is later transferred to the Statement of Profit and Loss at the end of each year as income, and debentures issued at a premium must always be redeemed at a premium. candidate.subject: accountancy
candidate.body: From the following, calculate the Trade Payables Turnover Ratio. Total purchases Rs 6,00,000 (no information about credit purchases is given); creditors at the end of the year Rs 70,000; bills payable at the end of the year Rs 30,000. Opening balances are not available.

options.text: 6 times
8.57 times
3 times
12 times

candidate.explanation: Since no credit purchases are given, total purchases of Rs 6,00,000 are taken as net purchases. Trade payables = creditors + bills payable = 70,000 + 30,000 = Rs 1,00,000, and dividing by 2 for the average gives Rs 50,000. Trade Payables Turnover Ratio = 6,00,000 / 50,000 = 12 times.

learning_objective.syllabus_unit: Analysis of Financial Statements: Accounting Ratios
learning_objective.objective: Calculate the trade payables turnover ratio.

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: Management is described as a goal-oriented process in which different organisations have different goals. Which of the following correctly pairs an organisation with its goal as given in this description?

options.text: The Spastics Society of India - to increase sales
A retail store - to increase sales
A retail store - to impart education to children with special needs
Every organisation - the same single common goal

candidate.explanation: The excerpt states that the goal of a retail store may be to increase sales, while the goal of The Spastics Society of India is to impart education to children with special needs. This makes options A and C reversed pairings. Option D is contradicted by the statement that different organisations have different goals.

learning_objective.objective: Explain the characteristics of management as a goal-oriented process

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: A petrol pump owner in India, a hospital administrator in Germany and a school principal in Japan all carry out the same managerial activities, although the way they do them differs because of culture, tradition and history. Which feature of management does this situation best illustrate?

options.text: Management is a continuous process, because functions are performed by all managers all the time
Management is a group activity, because it needs team work and coordination of individual effort
Management is a goal-oriented process, because the efforts of individuals are united towards organisational goals
Management is all pervasive, because managing activities are common to economic, social and political organisations

candidate.explanation: The excerpt says the activities of managing are common to all organisations, whether economic, social or political, and that managers in different countries do the same things in culturally different ways. This is the all pervasive feature. The other features concern simultaneous performance of functions, team work and goals, none of which the described situation turns on.

learning_objective.objective: Identify the features of management in a given situation

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: In a company, Ravi holds no managerial position. Yet colleagues follow his advice because of his personal qualities, and the group itself has chosen him as its spokesperson. Which statement correctly describes Ravi's influence?

options.text: It arises in the informal organisation, where authority arises out of personal qualities and leaders are chosen by the group
It arises in the formal organisation, where authority arises by virtue of position in management
It arises in the formal organisation, where managers are leaders and communication follows the scalar chain
It arises in the informal organisation, where authority is created by the management through company rules

candidate.explanation: The comparative view states that in an informal organisation authority arises out of personal qualities and leaders are chosen by the group. Ravi has no position, so authority by virtue of position (B) does not apply. Option C requires managers as leaders, and option D says management creates the authority, which is how the formal organisation works.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish between formal and informal organisation

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: In a manufacturing firm every employee has a written statement of duties. As a result, no member is unsure of the role to be played, and two employees never end up doing the same work twice. Which advantage of formal organisation is shown?

options.text: It is easier to fix responsibility since mutual relationships are clearly defined
It provides stability because behaviour of employees can be fairly predicted
There is no ambiguity in the role of each member as duties are specified, which avoids duplication of effort
Unity of command is maintained through an established chain of command

candidate.explanation: The excerpt lists as an advantage that there is no ambiguity in the role each member plays because duties are specified, which also helps avoid duplication of effort. This matches both facts in the case. The other advantages concern fixing responsibility, predictability of behaviour and the chain of command, none of which are described in the case.

learning_objective.objective: Explain the advantages of formal organisation

candidate.subject: business_studies
candidate.body: Meena buys 50 shares of a listed company from another investor, Arun, who wants to sell them. The company that originally issued the shares is not a party to this deal. In which market has this transaction taken place?

options.text: Secondary market, because the investor buys from another investor rather than from the issuer
Primary market, because the transaction allows the company to raise capital through issue of securities
Primary market, because shares are bought from an investor rather than from the issuer
Secondary market, because the company raises capital through issue of securities

candidate.explanation: The secondary market is where an investor buys or sells securities from another investor rather than the issuer, which is Meena's situation. The primary market is where companies raise capital by issuing securities, but here the issuing company is not a party, so B fails. Options C and D attach the wrong reason to each market.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish between primary market and secondary market

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: Under a fixed exchange rate system, the government changes the official exchange rate from Rs 75 per dollar to Rs 80 per dollar, so that one dollar now costs more rupees. According to the NCERT definitions, this government action is called:

options.text: Revaluation of the rupee
Devaluation of the rupee
Appreciation of the rupee
Floating of the exchange rate

candidate.explanation: In a fixed exchange rate system, a government action that increases the exchange rate (making the domestic currency cheaper) is Devaluation; here the rate rises from Rs 75 to Rs 80 per dollar. Revaluation is when the government decreases the exchange rate, which is the opposite of this change. Appreciation is defined for a flexible regime when the price of the rupee in dollars increases, but here the rupee has become cheaper and the change is a government action. A floating rate is determined by market forces of demand and supply, not by a government decision.

learning_objective.objective: Distinguish devaluation and revaluation in a fixed exchange rate system from appreciation in a flexible regime.

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: A bank is required to keep 20 per cent of its deposits as reserves. If the bank holds reserves of Rs 300 crore, what is the maximum amount of deposits that these reserves can support?

options.text: Rs 60 crore
Rs 240 crore
Rs 1,500 crore
Rs 375 crore

candidate.explanation: Reserves are 20 per cent of deposits, so deposits supported = 300 / 0.20 = Rs 1,500 crore, the same logic as reserves of Rs 100 supporting deposits of Rs 500. Rs 60 crore multiplies reserves by 0.20, which would be 20 per cent of the reserves rather than the deposits. Rs 240 crore takes 80 per cent of the reserves, and Rs 375 crore divides by 0.80; both wrongly treat 80 per cent, not 20 per cent, as the reserve share.

learning_objective.objective: Compute the deposits that a given amount of reserves can support from the reserve requirement.

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: The RBI sells government bonds worth Rs 500 crore in the open market to private individuals and institutions. According to the NCERT discussion of open market operations, what is the effect of this sale?

options.text: Reserves in the economy increase, so the money supply rises
Reserves in the economy fall, but the money supply is not affected
Neither reserves nor the money supply change, since only the ownership of bonds changes
Reserves in the economy fall, so the money supply is reduced

candidate.explanation: Selling of a bond by the RBI to private individuals or institutions leads to a reduction in the quantity of reserves and hence the money supply. It is the purchase of a bond by the RBI, paid for by cheque, that increases reserves and money supply, so the first option reverses the direction. The reduction in reserves is stated to lead to a fall in the money supply, which contradicts the second option, and the same statement contradicts the claim that nothing changes.

learning_objective.objective: Apply open market operations to predict their effect on reserves and money supply.

candidate.subject: economics
candidate.body: The government receives money in the following ways. Which one is a revenue receipt?

options.text: Corporation tax collected from firms, which the government never has to return
A loan raised by issuing bonds that the government must repay on maturity
Money borrowed from a foreign government, to be repaid with interest
Funds raised through securities that are redeemable after a fixed period

candidate.explanation: Revenue receipts are those that do not lead to a claim on the government, which is why they are termed non-redeemable, and they are divided into tax and non-tax revenues. Corporation tax is a tax revenue that the government never returns, so it creates no claim. The bond issue, the foreign loan and the redeemable securities are each stated to be repayable or redeemable, so they create a claim on the government and are not revenue receipts.

learning_objective.objective: Classify government receipts as revenue receipts using the criterion of no claim on the government.

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: According to the passage, what were students required to do each Friday during the trial?

options.text: Borrow two new books and grade the librarian's records
Return at least one book and write a short note about it
Return both books and discuss the notes with the librarian
Write a graded note on every book borrowed that week

candidate.explanation: The passage states that each Friday students returned at least one book and wrote a short note about it. They could borrow two books at a time, but returning both was not required. The librarian did not grade the notes, and discussing notes was only a later proposal.
candidate.passage_text: In a fictional school library, a trial reading programme ran for four weeks. Students could borrow two books at a time. Each Friday they returned at least one book and wrote a short note about it. The librarian recorded the number of books returned, but did not grade the notes. At the end of the trial, the borrowing records showed an increase in returns during the second and third weeks, followed by a small decrease in the fourth. The librarian said the records showed when books were returned, rather than how carefully they had been read. She proposed discussing a few notes with students before deciding whether to continue the programme. The proposal therefore combined a numerical record with evidence about the students’ experience.

learning_objective.objective: Identify specific factual details stated in a passage

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: Why did the report recommend comparing cups used per student before crediting the lending scheme for the larger fall in the second week?

options.text: Most borrowed cups were never returned, so the figures were unreliable
Disposable-cup use had not fallen at all during the first week
Lower attendance in the second week could by itself have reduced total cup use
The washable cups were issued without any refundable deposit

candidate.explanation: The passage says attendance was lower in the second week because one class was away, so fewer students could mean fewer cups used regardless of the scheme. Hence the report asked for a per-student comparison. The other options are contradicted: use fell in both weeks, most borrowed cups were returned, and a refundable deposit was charged.
candidate.passage_text: In this fictional report, a school canteen tested two ways of reducing disposable cups. During the first week, a sign asked students to bring their own cups. During the second, the canteen also lent washable cups against a refundable deposit. Disposable-cup use fell in both weeks, with a larger fall in the second. However, attendance was lower during the second week because one class was away. The report therefore recommended comparing cups used per student before attributing the larger fall to the lending scheme. It also recorded that most borrowed cups were returned. The trial suggested a possible benefit, while leaving the size of that benefit uncertain.

learning_objective.objective: Draw inferences about the reasoning behind a conclusion in a passage

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: Which statement best explains the grandfather's remark, "A promise includes care"?

options.text: Keeping a promise to bring the radio home includes protecting it, even if that means arriving late
Keeping a promise means reaching home before sunset whatever condition the radio is in
Mira should have asked the repairer to leave the electrical work unfinished
Mira should not have told him about the delay

candidate.explanation: Mira waited until the case was dry and covered the radio in the rain, accepting that she would miss sunset, and her grandfather approved. So he means that a promise covers looking after the radio, not just meeting the deadline. The passage says the electrical work was finished, and Mira deliberately telephoned to explain the delay.
candidate.passage_text: Mira had promised to bring her grandfather’s repaired radio home before sunset. At the workshop she found that the repairer had finished the electrical work, but the wooden case still needed to dry. “It will play,” he said, “but carrying it now may spoil the finish.” Mira looked at the dark clouds and then at the road to her village. She could reach home in time if she left immediately. Instead, she telephoned her grandfather and explained the delay. “A promise includes care,” he replied. She sat beside the workshop window until the case was ready. On the journey home the rain began, and she covered the radio with her coat. When she arrived, her grandfather switched it on. Neither of them mentioned the missed sunset; they listened quietly to the music.

learning_objective.objective: Infer the implied meaning of a character's statement in a narrative passage

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: What contrast does the tea seller notice for the first time at the end of the passage?

options.text: The trains had stopped running, just like the station clock
Travellers trusted the station clock more than their own watches
The clock was within his reach but he chose not to correct it
The still clock hands stood above a station where almost everything was moving

candidate.explanation: The last sentence states the hands stood still above a place where almost everything was moving, which the tea seller notices after the child watches the passing train. The trains were running, travellers checked their watches rather than relying on the clock, and the clock was beyond his reach.
candidate.passage_text: The station clock had stopped at ten past four. Each morning, travellers looked up, checked their watches and continued towards the platform. The tea seller never corrected the clock; it was beyond his reach. One afternoon, a child asked whether the trains had stopped too. He pointed to a train sliding past the far platform. Its windows caught the sun one after another. The child watched until it disappeared, then looked back at the clock. For the first time that day, the tea seller noticed the contrast himself: the hands stood still above a place where almost everything was moving.

learning_objective.objective: Interpret theme and contrast in a literary passage

candidate.subject: english
candidate.body: In the passage, the phrase "a scarce facility" most nearly refers to something that is

options.text: available in large numbers, so any group can use it whenever it wishes
limited in supply, so access to it has to be shared among users
kept for meetings longer than thirty minutes only
open only to regular visitors of the reading room

candidate.explanation: The reading room had a single discussion table, and reservation slots were introduced to share access to it, so "scarce" means limited in supply. The passage says unreserved time was open to any visitor, and meetings longer than thirty minutes were moved to a separate room.
candidate.passage_text: A fictional neighbourhood reading room introduced a reservation system for its single discussion table. Groups could book thirty-minute slots, but no group could book consecutive slots. Unreserved time remained available to any visitor. After a month, more groups had used the table, although some regular visitors complained that they could no longer hold long meetings there. The committee kept the reservation rule and offered a separate room for meetings lasting more than thirty minutes. Its decision aimed to share access to a scarce facility while accommodating a different need elsewhere. The report did not suggest that short meetings were inherently better than long ones.
